scores.design: Ensemble — many cards authored, one bundle compiled
scores.fatal_flaw: None. The nearest candidates are contained: (a) G-E4 reserved-key ownership is a real ceiling on fleet size, because voice/tools.py transitions by literal node name (_node('negotiate_ptp') at voice/tools.py:1183/1209), so only one member may own each RESERVED_NODE_KEY until Phase 5 refactors it — the design discloses this and phases it; (b) writing bot-to-bot hops into interaction_handoffs silently redefines the escalation metric, because db_bot_analytics.py:152, 209 and 339 all read EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM interaction_handoffs) as 'escalated to a human', and the reason column carries a CHECK constraint (sql/04_interactions.sql) that rejects 'specialist_route'. Ensemble migrates the CHECK but not the predicates, so escalation and containment rates — numbers that go into grievance MIS — inflate on the first specialist hop. One WHERE to_kind='bot' exclusion fixes it, but it must be in Phase 0.
scores.strongest_idea: The compiled flattened view plus G-E3. The author composes specialist cards on a canvas; the compiler flattens the reachable closure into one namespaced graph; the studio renders that exact compiled graph read-only so a compliance officer reviews the single path the borrower will traverse rather than a picture of intent. G-E3 then walks every path from the door's start to any node whose offer contains a non-read tool and requires verify_identity on it. That converts identity-before-writes from a prompt convention into a compile-time property — and because flow_walker runs the same compiled graph on WhatsApp, it is the only proposal that would close the verified text-path hole where bot_tools.py:300 passes identity_verified=True unconditionally into evaluate_authority.

scores.design: Bounded Fleet — compliance-boundary cards, skill-level specialists, one door, one release id
scores.fatal_flaw: G20's eval cache key is hash(card_hash, flow_hash, sorted skill_version_ids, grader_version) — and nothing in it is derived from prompt_versions.prompt, .persona, .guardrails, .voice or .tuning. The card is a column on that row (sql/09_bot_config.sql:110-125); the words are not in the card. So the single most common operator edit — rewriting the system prompt or the persona, rungs 0 and 1 of the ladder — republishes with G7 regression and G8 red-team passing on a cached report that never saw the new words, displayed to the author as 'pass · cached'. The design's own risks section warns about exactly this failure class for grader_version and then ships the key with a larger hole in it. It is a one-line fix, but as specified the sub-linearity in C6 is bought with the evidence a compliance officer signs.
scores.strongest_idea: G16 boundary_distinct: refuse a second production card whose persona hash, authority_profile, data_class and regulator_tags match an existing one, with the message 'this is a skill, not a card', and offer Promote-to-card when the boundary is genuinely new. It is the only mechanism in the three that enforces the customization ladder's rung-2/rung-3 wall (agent_transformation_phases.md section 3: fork a skill = linter + regression eval; compose a card = policy bindings + sandbox suite green) at publish time. Paired with authored skill activation replacing the hardcoded INTENT_TO_SKILL dict (verified at agent_core/skills/runtime.py:28-36), it lets an ops lead ship a twelfth specialist at rung 2 without creating a twelfth compliance surface.

scores.design: Sealed Fleet — Door, Specialists, one version per call
scores.fatal_flaw: G19 delta_redteam computes delta as (tools ∪ skills ∪ handoff edges) minus those present on any other fleet member — prompt and persona are not in it — while card.eval.inherit defaults to 'closure'. So an ops lead who clones Collections and rewrites only the persona and prompt into an aggressive chase script gets an empty delta, a red-team G19 reports as 'honestly skipped', and a regression inherited from a fleet suite that never saw those words. That is precisely the RBI fair-practices vector (harassment, mis-selling) and precisely the vector the ladder's rung-3 gate exists for. Worse, eval.inherit is an author-settable card field whose default is the cheap path: the design lets the author choose how much evaluation their own agent receives. Combined with resting identity-before-dispatch on card.human_gates — a field with no runtime consumer anywhere in the tree — the governance story is asserted rather than mechanised.
scores.strongest_idea: Deciding the canary once per call by hashing (fleet_version_id, customer_id) so every member of the call lands on the same side of the split. Today canary.pick_deployment_id hashes f'{bot_id}:{customer_id}' (agent_core/canary.py:73), so any design with per-card experiments can put Collections-canary and Insurance-baseline in one conversation and give a regulator a release id that resolves to a set. Sealed Fleet is the only one that closes that. Its hop-metric vocabulary is the second graft: hop.ttfb_ms, cached_tokens ratio read from usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, cover_ms (bridge audio duration minus first-token latency, positive means the miss was hidden) and misroute_rate (target hands back within two turns), all feeding the existing slo_miss rollback trigger.

best: Ensemble — many cards authored, one bundle compiled
graft: From Bounded Fleet — G16 boundary_distinct, adapted as an ensemble gate. Ensemble makes specialist cards cheap, which is its strength and its governance risk: nothing stops an ops lead creating twelve members where two compliance boundaries exist, and every extra member costs reserved-key contention (G-E4) and union-prefix tokens (G-E5). Add the refusal — identical persona hash, authority_profile, data_class and regulator_tags means 'this is a skill, not a card' — plus the Promote-to-card path. It is the compile-time expression of agent_transformation_phases.md section 3 and it costs Ensemble nothing it wants to keep.

From Bounded Fleet — authored skill activation (pack frontmatter: intents from the understanding vocabulary, objectives from flow_graph.OBJECTIVES, host-card node keys, variables over SESSION_VARIABLES) replacing the hardcoded INTENT_TO_SKILL dict at agent_core/skills/runtime.py:28-36. Ensemble replaces that dict with door expression edges, which forces a graph edge for what is a within-card specialisation and pushes authors toward creating members. Keep skills as the default specialisation and edges for real boundaries.

From Bounded Fleet — put a prompt_version content hash (prompt, persona, guardrails, voice, tuning) into the eval scope-diff key alongside card_hash and flow_hash. Ensemble's incremental Tier-3 slice diffs member card_hash/flow_hash against the previously published compiled bundle and inherits the same blind spot: a persona rewrite would ship on a slice that never re-tested it. Ensemble's nightly full run and its canary-to-100% full-suite requirement backstop this, but the canary itself would run unverified words at 10% of live traffic.

From Bounded Fleet — eval provenance in the Ship tab rendered as 'pass · cached r-… unchanged since 2026-08-30' with the report id, never as 'skipped'. Ensemble's compiler already distinguishes pass/fail/skipped (compile.py _eval_gate, G11's 'skip honestly, never fake-green'); a scoped or reused pass must say which report satisfied it, or a partial run reads as a full one to an auditor.

From Bounded Fleet — keep bot-to-bot hops out of interaction_handoffs, or exclude them from the escalation predicates in the same commit. Its separate handoff_events table is the correct instinct: interaction_handoffs currently means 'escalated to a human' in db_bot_analytics.py:152, 209 and 339, and is written only with to_kind='human' today (voice/persist.py:1183, db_routing.py:587, ops_screens.py:858).

From Sealed Fleet — decide the canary once per call, hashing (ensemble deployment id, customer_id). Ensemble gets this nearly free because one bot_deployments row per (door, environment) is already enforced by uq_bot_deployments_bot_env_active (sql/09_bot_config.sql:264), but write the rule down so a future multi-DEP ensemble cannot split-brain a single conversation across two versions.

From Sealed Fleet — the hop metrics, precisely because Ensemble claims a hop costs nothing. hop.ttfb_ms, cached_tokens ratio from usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, cover_ms and misroute_rate turn 'the prefix is byte-identical so the cache survives' from an assertion into a measurement, and misroute_rate is the routing-quality number a collections head can actually act on. Wire them to the existing slo_miss rollback trigger.

From Sealed Fleet — G17 door_readonly: an explicit tool allowlist for the door subgraph (verify_identity, get_customer_context, capture_call_goal, search_knowledge_base, set_contact_preference, add_customer_note, escalate_to_human and the transitions) so the routing surface can hold no write tool at all. G-E3 only requires that verify_identity sits on the path; G17 additionally guarantees the pre-identity portion of the graph cannot write, which is the cheaper and more legible control to show an inspector. It also gives the 'routing' key in REQUIRED_POLICY_KEYS (verified, schema.py:70-77) something to bind to.

From Sealed Fleet — consult_agent off the audio path, backed by the existing mcp_http/tasks.py enqueue/claim/finish queue, with results delivered as a developer message. This is how Ensemble answers the owner's 'agents communicate among themselves' for internal cards (supervisor-brief, a doc-verifier, a hardship-assessor) without putting a second reasoning agent on a sub-second turn, and without an event bus that TARGET-ARCHITECTURE section 6 refuses.

From Sealed Fleet — state the rule that outbound skips the door: the dialler already knows the objective, so the mission owner's subgraph is the entry and confirm_identity is its first node. Ensemble has the mechanism (compiled.missions plus entry_bindings) but not the prohibition, and nothing currently stops an author routing a dialled call through discover_intent.

From Sealed Fleet — Phase 0(a) as an immediate fix regardless of everything else: read the handoff allowlist from the published card on the bundle rather than defaults.card_for(). Verified live fail-open — voice/tools.py builds the allowlist from card_for(bot_id) and sets it to None on KeyError, and agent_core/tools/domain.py:1029 only enforces when 'allowlist is not None', so a tenant card that is not a first-party constant can hand off anywhere. bot_runtime.py:946-948 already does it correctly via bundle['agentCard']. Ensemble deletes the free-target tool eventually; this hole is open today and its Phase 0 ships first.
unverified_claims: All three designs assert that card.human_gates are enforced at execution. Nothing enforces them. A repo-wide search finds human_gates only at agent_core/cards/schema.py:389, agent_core/cards/defaults.py:131/150/171/312/328 and the frontend type at Habibi/src/api/agent-card.ts:317 — no consumer in voice/tools.py, bot_tools.py, agent_core/tools/grant.py or compile.py. Bounded Fleet names ToolGrant.may_execute, which is literally 'return name in self.allowed' (grant.py:121-123). Sealed Fleet names build_tools(bot_id=target), which does not read the field. Ensemble names 'the same handlers as today', which are none. The repo's own audit already records this (audit-reports/agent-studio-nextgen/raw/audit-graph-a4e1d7.json:212). Any design that keeps human_gates in its C3 story must ship the consumer in the same phase, or the field is a comment that reads as a control.

Sealed Fleet: 'the Door's existing HumanGate(handoff_to_agent, require=identity) means no specialist ever receives an unverified caller on voice' (defaults.py:171). That gate has no reader, so it guarantees nothing. Writes stay protected because session.identity_verified guards _require_customer (voice/tools.py:516-519) and every write tool re-checks it — but dispatch to a specialist is not a write, and an unverified caller can be handed across today and under the design as written.

Sealed Fleet: 'Every transcript turn and bot_tool_calls row carries bot_id and prompt_version_id (actor_bot_id already exists on tool calls).' interaction_transcript has no bot_id and no prompt_version_id (sql/04_interactions.sql:80-104) and none of the seven migration phases add them, so a spoken sentence that involved no tool call is attributable only by joining interaction_handoffs turn ranges. And actor_bot_id is not on bot_tool_calls — that table has agent_id and skill_id (sql/12_crosscutting.sql:148-150); actor_bot_id lives on a compliance-QA table (sql/07_compliance_qa.sql:24).

Ensemble and Sealed Fleet both route bot-to-bot hops into interaction_handoffs. Today that table means 'escalated to a human': it is written only with to_kind='human' (voice/persist.py:1183, db_routing.py:587, ops_screens.py:858) and three analytics queries read EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM interaction_handoffs h WHERE h.interaction_id = i.id) as the escalated flag for containment, per-intent and per-bot reporting (db_bot_analytics.py:152, 209, 339). Its reason column also carries a CHECK constraint admitting only eight human-escalation reasons, so an insert of 'specialist_route' fails until migrated — Ensemble migrates the CHECK, Sealed Fleet's Phase 0(b) does not mention it. Neither adds the to_kind='bot' exclusion, so the first specialist hop inflates the escalation rate a grievance report is built on.

Bounded Fleet: G20's eval cache content_key = hash(card_hash, flow_hash, sorted skill_version_ids, grader_version). Prompt, persona, guardrails, voice and tuning are columns on prompt_versions, not on the agent_card column (sql/09_bot_config.sql:110-125), so none of them are in the key and a persona or system-prompt edit passes G7 and G8 on a cached report. Ensemble's Tier-3 diff on member card_hash/flow_hash has the same omission, mitigated only by its nightly full run and its canary-to-100% full-suite requirement.

Sealed Fleet: G19's delta = (tools ∪ skills ∪ handoff edges) minus those on any other member excludes prompt and persona, and eval.inherit defaults to 'closure'. A clone whose only change is its words has an empty delta, a skipped red-team and an inherited regression. Nothing in the gate set catches a rewritten collections script.

Bounded Fleet and Sealed Fleet both warm the prefix produced by _system_instruction_from_bundle (voice/bot.py:78-104). On outbound that is not the prefix the call runs: voice/bot.py:566-577 appends mission_mod.briefing(_mission) to the system instruction and then does an in-place replace of 'inbound collections voice agent' with 'outbound collections voice agent', so the live system message is per-borrower and forks from the warmed one. Ensemble is the only design that removes both (its Phase 0 moves the briefing to a developer block and its deletions list covers bot.py:566-577), which also means Ensemble's cross-call prefix cache is a real, present-tense latency win independent of handoffs.

All three claim identity-before-writes survives every hop. On voice it does — session.identity_verified is set in the verify handler (voice/tools.py:840) and guards every write through _require_customer (:516-519), and it lives on VoiceSession rather than the card, so a card swap cannot clear it. On WhatsApp it does not: bot_tools.py:300 passes identity_verified=True unconditionally into evaluate_authority, and :627 derives it from customer_id != 'UNKNOWN-CALLER' rather than from a verification event. Only Ensemble's G-E3 would close this, because flow_walker runs the same compiled graph the gate walked. Sealed Fleet explicitly declines to build a text flow engine and offers 'prompt + identity human gates, exactly as today' as the mitigation — which is the phantom gate above.

Sealed Fleet's Phase 5 bus backend (one LLMWorker per card, LocalBus or RedisBus, a cross-process card_worker.py generalising the sidecar Phase 1 deleted, per-card model_profile) contradicts audit-reports/TARGET-ARCHITECTURE.md section 6, which refuses microservices and an event bus outright — 'the process split already exists and is correct', 'Postgres SKIP LOCKED is the broker' — without acknowledging the contradiction. The design also flags its own Pipecat dependency (whether FlowManager accepts an LLMSwitcher in 1.6.0) as unverified.

Sealed Fleet justifies replacing eval/run.py bot_id_for_suite by saying it will stop insurance-v1 reporting itself untested. That symptom is already fixed: the function's docstring (agent_core/eval/run.py:14-33) says resolving ownership from agent_card.eval.suite_id 'was tried and is wrong' because nine cards in this tenant name eval-regression-collections, that NULL is the truthful answer, and that the Evals-tab misreading was fixed in the tab. Bounded Fleet is the only design that reads this correctly and builds on the one-to-many sharing rather than contradicting it.

Ensemble's C1 claim that a hop adds no inference is sound for carry='brief' and carry='full' but rests on replace_developer folding safely under summarisation — the design lists this as its own risk (stale-fact assertion class VS-0D653BF9C3). The mechanism it reuses is real (voice/tools.py load_skill replaces the SKILL_BODY_PREFIX developer block), but no gate currently asserts that a replaced ACTIVE SPECIALIST block survives an LLMSummarizeContextFrame, so 'the hop costs nothing' is unverified until the conformance suite exists.

Ensemble's G-E4 (one member owns each RESERVED_NODE_KEY) is a genuine cap on how many specialists the owner can actually have, because voice/tools.py transitions to nodes by literal name (_node('negotiate_ptp'), _node('escalate_close'), flow_graph.RESERVED_NODE_KEYS at flow_graph.py:49). Until Phase 5 retires the name-based transitions, a second collections-shaped specialist cannot receive the built-in begin_* transitions. The design states this; the product owner should hear it as the real ceiling on 'twelve specialists', not as a detail.
